title: Permanent Daylight Saving Time
resolution: Resolved: The United States should adopt permanent daylight saving time.
summary: Many Americans want to stop changing the clocks twice a year. If we pick one time all year, should it be daylight saving time or standard time?

background.p: Most of the United States moves clocks forward an hour in spring (daylight saving time) and back in fall (standard time). In March 2022 the U.S. Senate passed the Sunshine Protection Act by unanimous consent, which would have made daylight saving time permanent, but the House did not pass it; the bill has been reintroduced since. Federal law currently lets states choose permanent *standard* time (as Hawaii and most of Arizona do) but not permanent daylight saving time.

The country tried year-round daylight saving time once before, starting in January 1974 during an energy crisis. Public support fell sharply during that dark winter, and Congress restored standard time for the winter months later that year. Today, sleep scientists, including the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, support ending clock changes but favor permanent standard time, saying it better matches the body's clock; supporters of permanent daylight saving time point to more evening daylight.

disputed.q: Which permanent time is better for health and safety?
positions: Sleep-medicine groups say standard time fits the body's clock better and avoids very dark winter mornings.
Supporters of daylight saving time cite studies linking evening light to fewer evening crashes and crimes and more outdoor activity.

terms.def: Clock time set by the time zone, used in winter; noon is close to when the sun is highest.
Clocks set one hour ahead of standard time, moving daylight from morning to evening.
The body's roughly 24-hour internal clock, set mainly by light.
The mismatch between the body's clock and the clock on the wall.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: End the clock switching and keep the extra hour of evening light all year.

args.claim: Ending the twice-yearly switch prevents its harms.
args.warrant: The spring change cuts an hour of sleep, and studies link the weeks after clock changes to more heart attacks and crashes. One permanent time ends that.
args.evidence: Studies linking the days after clock changes to more heart attacks and accidents; studies of the spring transition.
args.response: The negative answers that permanent standard time also ends the switch, so this argument doesn't favor daylight saving time.

args.claim: Evening light helps people be active and safe.
args.warrant: More daylight after school and work means more time outdoors, and darkness during the evening commute is linked to more pedestrian crashes and some crimes.
args.evidence: Studies of evening light and crime and traffic safety; research on physical activity and daylight.
args.response: The negative replies that the same hour is taken from the morning, putting children at bus stops in the dark.

args.warrant: Polls show many Americans prefer daylight saving time's later sunsets, and the Senate passed the bill unanimously, reflecting broad support.
args.evidence: Senate passage of the Sunshine Protection Act (March 2022); public opinion polls on time preferences.
args.response: The negative points out that in 1974 public support collapsed once people lived through dark winter mornings.

args.claim: Businesses and recreation benefit from later light.
args.warrant: Shops, parks, sports leagues and outdoor businesses do better when daylight lasts into the evening.
args.evidence: Industry studies of retail and recreation during daylight saving time; testimony from business groups.
args.response: The negative replies that economic gains are uncertain and don't outweigh health concerns.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Ending clock changes is good, but standard time, not daylight saving time, should be permanent.

args.claim: Standard time better matches the body's clock.
args.warrant: Morning light sets the body's internal clock. Permanent daylight saving time would leave many people waking and starting work or school in the dark for months, causing chronic "social jet lag."
args.evidence: American Academy of Sleep Medicine position statements; circadian research.
args.response: The affirmative answers that people adapt, and evening light offers its own health benefits through activity.

args.claim: Winter mornings would be very dark.
args.warrant: Under permanent daylight saving time, winter sunrise would come after 8 a.m. in much of the country and after 9 a.m. in some northern places, so children would wait for buses and walk to school in the dark.
args.evidence: AASM analysis of winter sunrise times; sunrise tables for northern cities.
args.response: The affirmative replies that schools can adjust start times, and evening darkness is also dangerous.

args.claim: The country tried it and reversed course.
args.warrant: In 1974, year-round daylight saving time was popular until people lived through a dark winter; support fell and Congress changed the law within the year.
args.evidence: History of the Emergency Daylight Saving Time Energy Conservation Act of 1973 and its repeal.
args.response: The affirmative argues that was a sudden emergency change, and today's debate is more informed.

args.claim: Health and safety groups favor standard time.
args.warrant: When sleep doctors, the National Safety Council and the National PTA agree, their combined expertise on health and children's safety deserves weight.
args.evidence: AASM statement supported by more than a dozen organizations, as reported in 2022.
args.response: The affirmative replies that expert groups disagree on how to weigh evening safety and activity, and voters also deserve a say.

strawmen.strawman: They just want more time to play outside in summer.
strawmen.why: Supporters also cite the harms of clock changes and evening safety.
strawmen.steelman: Ending the switch prevents its harms, and keeping evening light all year supports activity, safety and the economy, which is why the Senate passed it unanimously.

strawmen.strawman: They want to keep changing the clocks forever.
strawmen.why: Most opponents of permanent DST want to end the switch too, but on standard time.
strawmen.steelman: End the switch, but on standard time, which matches the body's clock and avoids dark winter mornings, as sleep experts recommend and as 1974 showed.

weak.arg: Daylight saving time gives us more daylight.
weak.why: It moves daylight from morning to evening; the total is the same.
A common myth; farmers generally opposed it. It also argues against your own side.
